## What this notebook does

We ask whether **armed conflict lowers school completion** — at the primary, lower
secondary and upper secondary levels. The design starts from
[Jawad et al. (2021, *PLOS Medicine*)](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.1003810)
— a country-year panel with two-way fixed effects (country + year) and
country-clustered standard errors, as in our mortality analysis
(`2_analyze_mortality.Rmd`) — but the outcome forces one important adaptation.

**The completion rate is measured on people who left the relevant age years ago.**
UNESCO's completion rate — an official SDG 4.1.2 indicator — is the share of people
aged **3 to 5 years older than the official completion age** of a school level who
have finished that level. The three-to-five-year allowance exists because in many
countries children start school late or repeat grades, so measuring completion right
at the nominal completion age would miss them. The consequence for us: the people
behind a completion rate published for year $Y$ were **in school during a window of
past years**, and that window — not year $Y$ — is when conflict could have pushed
them out of school.

A worked example. Suppose primary school in some country runs from age 6 to age 11
(six grades). The primary completion rate for year $Y$ is then measured on 14- to
16-year-olds. The **oldest** of them (16) could have started primary as early as year
$Y-10$; the **youngest** (14) left the primary age range in year $Y-3$. So the
in-school exposure window is $Y-10$ to $Y-3$. In general, for a level lasting $d$
years the window is

$$Y-(d+4) \;\;\text{to}\;\; Y-3,$$

which spans $d+2$ calendar years. Note that the school *entrance* age drops out of
the formula: because the reference ages are pegged to the completion age, only the
level's **duration** matters — and durations differ across countries and levels, so
each country-year-level observation gets its own window.

Within that window we measure conflict in **four ways**, echoing Jawad's
specifications:

1. `any_confl` — did conflict occur at any point in the window? (1 if any window
   year had ≥ 25 battle-related deaths, the standard UCDP threshold for an active
   conflict);
2. `cum_deaths_p100k` — cumulative intensity: total battle deaths per 100,000
   population summed over the window;
3. `avg_deaths_p100k` — average intensity: battle deaths per 100,000 per year,
   i.e. the mean over the window;
4. `confl_quint` — the cumulative measure split into quintiles among
   conflict-affected observations, with "no conflict in the window" as the
   reference group.

Two further design notes, carried over from the stunting analysis
(`4_analyze_stunting.Rmd`):

- **Exposure is built on the full annual conflict grid first** (every country-year
  1989–2024, with zeros in peaceful years), and only then attached to the completion
  observations — so gaps in the outcome can never corrupt the exposure.
- **Conflict variation is concentrated in a handful of countries**, so alongside the
  conventional country-clustered standard errors we report a **wild cluster
  bootstrap**, which remains honest when the number of truly informative countries
  is small.

Exposure is **battle deaths per 100,000 population** from UCDP GED, pre-built in
`1_build_master.R`. We use the master as-is.

```{r libraries}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(fixest)
library(fwildclusterboot)
library(effClust)
library(knitr)
```

## The data

```{r load-master}
master <- readRDS(here("data_derived", "pillar4_master.rds"))

# Covariate set held constant across all models (same as the other Pillar 4 analyses).
setFixest_fml(..ctrls = ~ log_gdp_pc + age_dep_ratio + pct_urban + pop_density +
                male_schooling + temperature + rainfall + earthquake + drought)
ctrls <- c("log_gdp_pc", "age_dep_ratio", "pct_urban", "pop_density",
           "male_schooling", "temperature", "rainfall", "earthquake", "drought")
```

### Completion rates

UNESCO models completion from all available household surveys and censuses into a
smooth annual series per country and level, using the Adjusted Bayesian Completion
Rates (ABCR) model of
[Dharamshi et al. (2022, *JRSS Series C*)](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssc.12595);
what that modelling implies for our estimates is taken up in the caveats at the end
of this notebook. We use the headline estimate (`projected3t5`, the share completing
within 3–5 years above the completion age — the SDG definition), both sexes
combined. Rates are percentages.

```{r load-cr}
cr <- read_csv(here("data", "Pillar 4", "outcomes",
                    "UNESCO Completion Rate Estimates.csv"),
               show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(outcome == "projected3t5", sex == "total",
         level %in% c("prim", "lsec", "usec")) |>
  mutate(iso3, year, level, cr = value, .keep = "none")
```

### How long is each school level?

Level durations come from the UNESCO school-calendar data: primary duration is the
gap between the official entrance ages to primary and lower secondary; lower
secondary duration is the gap between the lower- and upper-secondary entrance ages;
upper secondary duration is reported directly. Durations are country-**and**-year
specific (education reforms change them), so for the completion rate of year $Y$ we
use the duration in force in year $Y-4$ — the midpoint of the years ($Y-5$ to $Y-3$)
in which the measured cohort was finishing the level. Where a country's calendar
series has gaps we carry the nearest reported value across them.

```{r durations}
cal <- read_excel(here("data", "UNESCO info", "school_age_calendar_info.xlsx"))

durations <- cal |>
  filter(indicatorId %in% c("299905", "999975", "999977", "999978")) |>
  select(iso3 = geoUnit, year, indicatorId, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorId, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(prim = `999975` - `299905`,   # entrance-age gap primary -> lower sec
         lsec = `999977` - `999975`,   # entrance-age gap lower sec -> upper sec
         usec = `999978`) |>           # reported directly
  select(iso3, year, prim, lsec, usec) |>
  pivot_longer(c(prim, lsec, usec), names_to = "level", values_to = "dur") |>
  filter(!is.na(dur), dur >= 1) |>
  group_by(iso3, level) |>
  complete(year = 1990:2024) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  fill(dur, .direction = "downup") |>
  ungroup()

durations |>
  filter(year == 2016) |>   # the calendar year feeding the 2020 completion rates
  count(level, dur) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = dur, values_from = n, names_prefix = "duration ") |>
  kable(caption = "Countries by level duration (as of 2016)")
```

### The exposure window

Each completion observation gets its window $Y-(d+4)$ to $Y-3$, and we aggregate the
annual conflict series across it. An observation is kept only if **every** window
year is covered by the conflict data (1989–2024); together with the analysis start
in 2000 (below), every retained observation has a complete window.

```{r windows}
crd <- cr |>
  mutate(cal_year = year - 4) |>
  inner_join(durations |> rename(cal_year = year),
             by = c("iso3", "level", "cal_year")) |>
  mutate(win_lo = year - (dur + 4), win_hi = year - 3)

grid <- master |>
  mutate(gyear = year, .keep = "unused") |>
  select(iso3, gyear, battle_deaths, battle_deaths_p100k)

expo <- crd |>
  inner_join(grid, by = join_by(iso3, win_lo <= gyear, win_hi >= gyear)) |>
  summarise(n_win = n(),
            any_confl = as.integer(any(battle_deaths >= 25)),
            cum_deaths_p100k = sum(battle_deaths_p100k),
            avg_deaths_p100k = mean(battle_deaths_p100k),
            .by = c(iso3, year, level, cr, dur, win_lo, win_hi)) |>
  filter(n_win == dur + 2)
```

We then attach the covariates (measured in the outcome year $Y$), restrict the
analysis to completion rates from **2000** on, and build the quintile variable.
Quintile cut-points are computed within each level over the observations with any
conflict deaths in the window; window-peaceful observations form the reference
group ("none").

```{r panel}
covars <- master |>
  mutate(log_gdp_pc = log(gdp_pc)) |>
  select(iso3, year, all_of(ctrls))

dta <- expo |>
  left_join(covars, by = c("iso3", "year")) |>
  filter(year >= 2000) |>
  group_by(level) |>
  mutate(confl_quint = {
    qb <- quantile(cum_deaths_p100k[cum_deaths_p100k > 0], probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2))
    factor(if_else(cum_deaths_p100k > 0,
                   as.character(cut(cum_deaths_p100k, breaks = qb,
                                    labels = paste0("Q", 1:5),
                                    include.lowest = TRUE)),
                   "none"),
           levels = c("none", paste0("Q", 1:5)))
  }) |>
  ungroup()
```

### The estimation sample

We keep rows with a completion rate, a complete window and complete covariates, and
then drop **singleton fixed-effect groups** — countries (or years) left with a
single observation. A lone observation is perfectly absorbed by its own fixed
effect, contributes nothing, and breaks the wild cluster bootstrap's
pre-processing; we drop such groups iteratively until the sample is stable. Because
all four exposure measures are computed from the same window, they are available
for exactly the same rows — so within a level, **all four specifications run on the
identical sample**.

```{r sample}
MakeSample <- function(data, xvars) {
  s <- data |>
    filter(!is.na(cr), if_all(all_of(c(xvars, ctrls)), \(x) !is.na(x)))
  repeat {
    n0 <- nrow(s)
    s <- s |>
      add_count(iso3, name = "n_iso") |> filter(n_iso >= 2) |>
      add_count(year, name = "n_yr")  |> filter(n_yr  >= 2) |>
      select(-n_iso, -n_yr)
    if (nrow(s) == n0) break
  }
  s |> mutate(iso3 = factor(iso3), year = factor(year))
}

exposures <- c("any_confl", "cum_deaths_p100k", "avg_deaths_p100k", "confl_quint")

d_prim <- MakeSample(filter(dta, level == "prim"), exposures)
d_lsec <- MakeSample(filter(dta, level == "lsec"), exposures)
d_usec <- MakeSample(filter(dta, level == "usec"), exposures)

tibble(
  Level = c("Primary", "Lower secondary", "Upper secondary"),
  Observations = c(nrow(d_prim), nrow(d_lsec), nrow(d_usec)),
  Countries = c(n_distinct(d_prim$iso3), n_distinct(d_lsec$iso3),
                n_distinct(d_usec$iso3)),
  `First year` = map_dbl(list(d_prim, d_lsec, d_usec),
                         \(d) min(as.integer(as.character(d$year)))),
  `Last year` = map_dbl(list(d_prim, d_lsec, d_usec),
                        \(d) max(as.integer(as.character(d$year))))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Estimation samples")
```

Unlike the survey-only stunting and wasting outcomes, the completion series is a
**dense modelled panel** — nearly every country contributes every year. That makes
the samples large, but the observations within a country are strongly serially
dependent by construction (the model smooths across years), which is one more
reason to lean on country-clustered inference throughout.

## Descriptive picture

```{r fig-scatter, fig.height=4}
dta |>
  filter(cum_deaths_p100k > 0) |>
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = c("prim", "lsec", "usec"),
                        labels = c("Primary", "Lower secondary",
                                   "Upper secondary"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(cum_deaths_p100k, cr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, colour = "#457b9d") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#c1121f", se = TRUE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  facet_wrap(~level) +
  labs(title = "School completion vs. cumulative conflict exposure",
       subtitle = "Conflict-affected observations only (log x-axis); raw, before fixed effects",
       x = "Cumulative battle deaths per 100,000 over the window (log scale)",
       y = "Completion rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The raw downward slopes likely reflect the fact that poorer countries have both
more conflict and lower completion. The fixed-effects models strip out fixed
country differences and global year shocks, and identify the effect from
**within-country** movement in conflict exposure over time.

## Models

For each level we regress the completion rate on one conflict measure at a time,
plus the covariates, with country and year fixed effects and country-clustered
standard errors. Coefficients are in **percentage points of the completion rate**:
for the binary measure, the difference associated with having any conflict in the
window; for the cumulative (average) measure, the change per one additional battle
death per 100,000 summed over the window (per year); for the quintiles, the
difference between each intensity band and window-peaceful observations.

### Primary

```{r models-prim}
m_prim_bin   <- feols(cr ~ any_confl + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_prim, cluster = ~iso3)
m_prim_cum   <- feols(cr ~ cum_deaths_p100k + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_prim, cluster = ~iso3)
m_prim_avg   <- feols(cr ~ avg_deaths_p100k + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_prim, cluster = ~iso3)
m_prim_quint <- feols(cr ~ confl_quint + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_prim, cluster = ~iso3)

etable(m_prim_bin, m_prim_cum, m_prim_avg, m_prim_quint,
       keep = c("confl", "deaths"),
       headers = c("Binary", "Cumulative", "Average", "Quintiles"))
```

### Lower secondary

```{r models-lsec}
m_lsec_bin   <- feols(cr ~ any_confl        + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_lsec, cluster = ~iso3)
m_lsec_cum   <- feols(cr ~ cum_deaths_p100k + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_lsec, cluster = ~iso3)
m_lsec_avg   <- feols(cr ~ avg_deaths_p100k + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_lsec, cluster = ~iso3)
m_lsec_quint <- feols(cr ~ confl_quint      + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_lsec, cluster = ~iso3)

etable(m_lsec_bin, m_lsec_cum, m_lsec_avg, m_lsec_quint,
       keep = c("confl", "deaths"),
       headers = c("Binary", "Cumulative", "Average", "Quintiles"))
```

### Upper secondary

```{r models-usec}
m_usec_bin   <- feols(cr ~ any_confl        + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_usec, cluster = ~iso3)
m_usec_cum   <- feols(cr ~ cum_deaths_p100k + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_usec, cluster = ~iso3)
m_usec_avg   <- feols(cr ~ avg_deaths_p100k + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_usec, cluster = ~iso3)
m_usec_quint <- feols(cr ~ confl_quint      + ..ctrls | iso3 + year,
                      data = d_usec, cluster = ~iso3)

etable(m_usec_bin, m_usec_cum, m_usec_avg, m_usec_quint,
       keep = c("confl", "deaths"),
       headers = c("Binary", "Cumulative", "Average", "Quintiles"))
```

## Inference: how many real clusters, and a wild cluster bootstrap

### Effective-cluster diagnostic

The conventional standard errors treat every country as an independent source of information. But the conflict coefficient is identified only by countries whose conflict exposure during the in-school window actually *changes* from one observation to the next — where it is constant (most obviously, always zero), the country fixed effect absorbs it entirely. The amount of change is wildly unequal — a few intense conflicts dominate. We summarise this per level: the number of countries; how many are ever exposed in-sample; how many carry any within-country variation in the cumulative exposure (only these identify the coefficient); and a Herfindahl-style **effective number of clusters**, based on each country's share of the within-country variance of the exposure. The latter is a heuristic measure based on the inverse of Herfindahl-Hirschman index of concentration used in economics. It answers the question "Assuming variation were evenly distributed among equal-sized clusters, how many clusters would be needed to have the observed level of variation concentration?" When the effective number is far below the nominal one, analytic *t*-statistics can be overconfident.

```{r cluster-diagnostic}
ClusterDiag <- function(d) {
  cl <- d |>
    group_by(iso3) |>
    summarise(within_ss = sum((cum_deaths_p100k - mean(cum_deaths_p100k))^2),
              ever_exposed = any(cum_deaths_p100k > 0), .groups = "drop")
  c(countries    = nrow(cl),
    ever_exposed = sum(cl$ever_exposed),
    identifying  = sum(cl$within_ss > 1e-12),   # Testing if >0; 1e-12 is an arbitrary epsilon to weed out rounding residues
    effective    = round(sum(cl$within_ss)^2 / sum(cl$within_ss^2), 1))
}

list(Primary = d_prim, `Lower secondary` = d_lsec,
     `Upper secondary` = d_usec) |>
  map(ClusterDiag) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "Level") |>
  rename(`Countries (nominal clusters)` = countries,
         `Ever exposed in window` = ever_exposed,
         `With exposure variation (identifying)` = identifying,
         `Effective number of clusters` = effective) |>
  kable(caption = "How much independent information identifies the conflict effect?")
```

The same, but using the `effClust` package this time. 
```{r}
effClust(m_prim_cum, cluster = ~iso3)
```

### Wild cluster bootstrap

The technique comes from
[Cameron, Gelbach and Miller (2008, *Review of Economics and Statistics*)](https://doi.org/10.1162/rest.90.3.414).
The idea, in plain terms: rather than trusting a textbook standard-error formula
whose guarantees hold only when many clusters carry information, we rebuild the
dataset thousands of times — each time keeping the fitted model but randomly
flipping the sign of each country's *entire block* of residuals — and re-estimate
the conflict coefficient in every rebuilt dataset under the assumption that the
true effect is zero. If the coefficient we actually estimated would look
unremarkable among those thousands of zero-effect re-creations, we cannot call it
significant. Flipping residuals country-by-country — never observation by
observation — preserves whatever correlation exists inside each country, and
Cameron and colleagues show this yields far more accurate *p*-values than analytic
clustered standard errors when only a few clusters dominate — precisely our
situation. The six-value "Webb weights" we use in place of simple sign flips are a
refinement for very small effective cluster counts, due to
[Webb (2023, *Canadian Journal of Economics*)](https://doi.org/10.1111/caje.12661).

So the parameters are: Webb 6-point weights, restricted null, 9,999 replications, clustered by country,
with the year fixed effect held fixed in the resampling. We bootstrap the binary,
cumulative and average coefficients, and — for the quintile specification — the
top-intensity contrast (Q5 vs none), where any real effect should be most visible.
Bootstrap *p*-values and confidence intervals are reported **alongside** the
analytic ones.

```{r boottest}
BootTable <- function(models, caption) {
  params <- c(Binary = "any_confl", Cumulative = "cum_deaths_p100k",
              Average = "avg_deaths_p100k", Quintiles = "confl_quintQ5")
  imap(params, \(param, spec) {
    m <- models[[spec]]
    set.seed(1); dqrng::dqset.seed(1)
    bt <- boottest(m, param = param, clustid = ~iso3,
                   fe = "year", B = 9999, type = "webb")
    ct <- coeftable(m)[param, ]
    tibble(
      Specification = if (spec == "Quintiles") "Quintiles (Q5 vs none)" else spec,
      Estimate      = round(ct[["Estimate"]], 4),
      `Analytic p`  = round(ct[["Pr(>|t|)"]], 4),
      `Bootstrap p` = round(bt$p_val, 4),
      `Boot 2.5%`   = round(bt$conf_int[1], 4),
      `Boot 97.5%`  = round(bt$conf_int[2], 4)
    )
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    kable(caption = caption)
}
```

```{r boot-prim}
BootTable(list(Binary = m_prim_bin, Cumulative = m_prim_cum,
               Average = m_prim_avg, Quintiles = m_prim_quint),
          "Primary: analytic vs wild-cluster-bootstrap inference")
```

```{r boot-lsec}
BootTable(list(Binary = m_lsec_bin, Cumulative = m_lsec_cum,
               Average = m_lsec_avg, Quintiles = m_lsec_quint),
          "Lower secondary: analytic vs wild-cluster-bootstrap inference")
```

```{r boot-usec}
BootTable(list(Binary = m_usec_bin, Cumulative = m_usec_cum,
               Average = m_usec_avg, Quintiles = m_usec_quint),
          "Upper secondary: analytic vs wild-cluster-bootstrap inference")
```

## Interpretation and caveats

- **What we find: no robust association, at any level, in any specification.** Net
  of fixed country and year differences, none of the twelve estimates survives the
  wild cluster bootstrap. The cautionary tale is the continuous primary-level
  estimates: the cumulative and average intensity coefficients carry analytic
  *p*-values near zero, yet the bootstrap sends both to *p* ≈ 0.6. At upper
  secondary the analytically "significant" coefficients even have the *wrong*
  (positive) sign — a further hint that these are artefacts of overconfident
  standard errors, not signal. The binary and quintile measures are null under both
  methods everywhere.
- **Why the analytic and bootstrap answers disagree so sharply.** Roughly a hundred
  countries per level are conflict-exposed in-window, but the within-country
  variance of cumulative exposure is so concentrated that the **effective** number
  of clusters is about **one**. With one dominant cluster, conventional clustered
  *t*-statistics behave as if they had ~160 independent observations when they
  effectively have one; the wild cluster bootstrap is the honest inference in that
  situation, and its verdict — null — is the one we report.
- **The outcome is a model, not a raw measurement.** The completion series is
  produced by UNESCO's Adjusted Bayesian Completion Rates (ABCR) model
  ([Dharamshi et al., 2022, *JRSS Series C*](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssc.12595)),
  which consolidates roughly 700 census and household-survey datasets — surveys
  arrive every 3–5 years at best — into one smooth annual series per country and
  level. Its authors are explicit that model-based estimates "should not be
  mistaken for the actual measure," and four features of the model matter for how
  our estimates should be read:
  - *Between surveys, the series is filled in by a trend model.* The underlying
    trend is a time-series process (an ARIMA(1,1,0) with a country-specific,
    deliberately positive long-run drift, fitted on the probit scale). The model
    does let shocks to the *level* of completion persist — the drop after the 1994
    Rwandan genocide, straddled by surveys, is visibly captured — but a short dip
    that no survey directly observed is smoothed through, and the most recent
    years of the series are projections carried by each country's drift (at
    publication the median country's latest survey was 2017). Both features
    *attenuate* exactly the short, sharp disruptions conflict causes, making our
    estimates conservative for them.
  - *Reconstructing the past assumes conflict does not remove people selectively.*
    Because surveys are rare, the model backcasts up to 20 years of completion
    rates from older respondents' reports, assuming completers and non-completers
    are equally likely to have survived and stayed in the country. War violates
    this assumption in one direction: if those pushed out of school are also more
    likely to die or flee, the survivors interviewed later overstate their
    cohort's completion — and the measurement is most fragile precisely in the
    conflict-affected observations that identify our coefficient.
  - *People invisible to every survey stay invisible.* The model can identify only
    the *relative* bias of one survey against another; groups missed by all
    household sampling frames — displaced families, street children, populations
    outside households — cannot be corrected for, as the authors note. Conflict
    swells exactly these groups.
  - *The published uncertainty is discarded.* The estimates come with credible
    intervals that are widest where surveys are scarce — disproportionately
    conflict-affected countries — but our regressions weight every point estimate
    equally.
- **Bracket mismatch with the source model.** For internal consistency the ABCR
  model pins each country's reference ages to its *most recent* official entry age
  and duration, whereas our exposure windows let durations vary by year. Where a
  reform changed a level's length, the cohort UNESCO measured and the window we
  build for it can therefore disagree by a year or two.
- **The window covers the level itself.** For lower and upper secondary, conflict
  during a cohort's *earlier* schooling could also matter (a child pushed out of
  primary school never reaches secondary); our windows do not count that earlier
  exposure, so each level's estimate captures exposure during that level only.
- **Durations are approximations.** Level durations are assigned from the calendar
  in force in year $Y-4$ and gap-filled where the calendar series is incomplete;
  members of the same measured cohort can also straddle a reform.
- **Ecological design.** As throughout Pillar 4, this is a country-level analysis:
  it speaks to national averages, not to the experience of individual
  conflict-exposed children.
```
